data-platform.analytics-logic: Complex business rules, aggregations, and reporting transformations were implemented at the RDS layer using database views to reduce BI dataset complexity and stabilize query patterns.
data-platform.bi-layer: Simple report-specific expressions were delegated to QuickSight calculated fields, keeping the visualization layer lightweight and avoiding unnecessary duplication of heavy aggregation logic.
data-platform.platform: Reporting workloads were isolated from the transactional path through view-based models, SPICE usage, and dedicated read-oriented strategies to support operational analytics without destabilizing OLTP behavior.

performance-opt.heavy-report-opt: Expensive district-wide joins were reduced by isolating school metadata into DynamoDB and synchronizing relational metadata into a read-optimized structure.
performance-opt.spice: Daily summary reports were moved to SPICE with scheduled refresh, eliminating unnecessary real-time query load on the source database.
performance-opt.query-tuning: Composite indexes, execution plan analysis, join restructuring, and view-based query shaping reduced dashboard latency and improved overall reporting responsiveness.

design.a: Reports were built in QuickSight and embedded into the application using secure URLs generated through .NET API and Lambda orchestration.
design.b: Access control was enforced through API-level authorization, role-aware filtering, and parameterized tenant scoping for school-level and district-level users.
design.c: This architecture maintained secure multi-tenant isolation while keeping the reporting experience fully embedded.

strategy.a: QuickSight session pricing made high-frequency report access operationally expensive at scale.
strategy.b: A snapshot rendering pipeline was introduced: if a requested report snapshot already existed, the platform served the cached visual output instead of creating a new BI session.
strategy.c: Headless browser capture + S3 storage dramatically reduced session creation while preserving visual equivalence for non-interactive report scenarios.

header.title: SQL Tuning Advisor
header.desc: Designed and implemented an automated SQL tuning system by reverse-engineering Oracle SQL Tuning Advisor. The system analyzes slow SQL and generates optimization recommendations including SQL Profile, index suggestions, statistics fixes, and SQL rewrites.

overview.title: Overview
overview.desc1: Oracle SQL Tuning Advisor is an automated SQL performance analysis and optimization system provided by Oracle Database.
overview.desc2: This project reverse-engineered that workflow and implemented an Oracle-style SQL tuning automation framework, including task lifecycle management, advisor metadata tables, analysis modules, report generation, and SQL Profile acceptance flow.
overview.desc3: In practical terms, this can be understood as an advanced internal system that automates EXPLAIN analysis + optimizer tuning + recommendation generation.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.desc: The key objective of this project was not just manual SQL tuning, but automation of SQL tuning workflows: converting optimizer knowledge and performance diagnostics into a repeatable advisor system that can create, execute, analyze, and report tuning tasks.

stat.title: 1. Statistics Analysis
stat.desc: Detects stale or missing statistics that lead to incorrect execution plans.

profiling.title: 2. SQL Profiling
profiling.desc: Compares estimated vs actual row count patterns and generates profile-based recommendations to improve optimizer decision quality.

access.title: 3. Access Path Analysis
access.desc: Evaluates whether Full Scan or Index Scan is more appropriate and suggests access-path improvements.

structure.title: 4. SQL Structure Analysis
structure.desc: Detects query patterns that degrade performance and provides rewrite recommendations.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.desc: Implemented an Oracle-style SQL Tuning Advisor by reverse engineering internal architecture, including task lifecycle, analysis modules, recommendation logic, report generation, and SQL Profile acceptance flow.

milestone.c: • Design advisor packages, system tables, and views
milestone.d: • Build tuning task execution and report generation system

feature.e: • Expensive operation detection (NOT IN, UNION, join issues)

package.title: 1. Package Design
package.desc: The advisor was designed around multiple internal packages, following the Oracle-style separation between public APIs, internal execution logic, and low-level utility subprograms.

item1.a: • Public package that exposes the main advisor lifecycle APIs
item1.b: • Includes procedures/functions for CREATE, EXECUTE, REPORT, and ACCEPT SQL PROFILE
item1.c: • Serves as the main user-facing interface for tuning task management

item2.a: • Internal execution package responsible for the detailed analysis steps during tuning task execution
item2.b: • Encapsulates advisor workflow logic such as statistics analysis, access path analysis, and structural SQL checks
item2.c: • Separates internal execution behavior from the public package API

item3.a: • Utility package for subprograms that need lower-level implementation
item3.b: • Designed to isolate logic better suited for C/C++-level implementation
item3.c: • Helps keep advisor package logic modular and maintainable

table.title: 2. System Tables
table.desc: The advisor required dedicated system metadata tables created during DB booting, along with DBA-style views for visibility into definitions, tasks, objects, executions, and logs.

system_tables.definitions: • ADVISOR_DEFINITIONS: Stores metadata for advisor categories such as ADDM, SQL Access Advisor, Undo Advisor, SQL Tuning Advisor, and SQL Workload Manager
system_tables.tasks: • ADVISOR_TASKS: Stores and manages each advisor execution unit as a task
system_tables.objects: • ADVISOR_OBJECTS: Stores task-related objects by object_id and object_name
system_tables.logs: • ADVISOR_LOGS: Records step-by-step logging of advisor execution and tuning progress

table.footer: This metadata layer was critical for implementing task lifecycle persistence, execution traceability, and report generation

create.title: 3. Create Tuning Task
create.a: • Accepts user inputs such as sql_id, scope, task_name, time_limit, and related tuning parameters
create.b: • Generates default values for missing optional inputs
create.c: • Performs validation checks on input arguments
create.d: • Persists validated inputs and generated metadata into advisor system tables
create.e: • Establishes the initial lifecycle state of the tuning task

execute.title: 4. Execute Tuning Task
execute.desc: The execution phase was designed as a multi-step analysis pipeline that automatically inspects optimizer-related causes of SQL performance issues.

stat.a: • Detects missing or stale statistics on tables and indexes
stat.b: • Identifies cases where poor optimizer estimates may be caused by statistics quality issues

access.a: • Evaluates whether current access paths are cost-optimal with and without indexes
access.b: • Generates guidance on access path improvement
access.c: • Can recommend running SQL Access Advisor when index-oriented design changes are needed

structure.a: • Detects query patterns known to cause performance degradation at syntax / semantic analysis stage
structure.b: • Recommends replacing NOT IN with NOT EXISTS
structure.c: • Recommends replacing UNION with UNION ALL where appropriate
structure.d: • Detects datatype mismatch between indexed columns and WHERE clause predicates
structure.e: • Detects missing join conditions that indicate design mistakes or hidden Cartesian effects

report.a: • Aggregates advisor findings from execution logs, analysis output, and recommendation records
report.b: • Produces structured tuning reports for users
report.c: • Summarizes actionable items such as statistics collection, SQL rewrite, alternative plan, and SQL Profile usage
report.d: • Designed as the final user-facing output of the tuning task lifecycle

profile.a: • Supports applying approved SQL Profile recommendations to the target SQL
profile.b: • Connects advisor recommendation results to optimizer execution behavior
profile.c: • Bridges analysis output with actual runtime performance improvement

summary.a: • Public API Layer: DBMS_SQLTUNE package for task creation, execution, reporting, and SQL Profile acceptance
summary.b: • Internal Execution Layer: DBMS_SQLTUNE_INTERNAL package for advisor pipeline and analysis execution
summary.c: • Utility Layer: C/C++-oriented utility package for low-level subprogram support
summary.d: • Metadata Layer: Advisor system tables and DBA views for definitions, tasks, objects, logs, and executions
summary.e: • Recommendation Layer: Statistics, access path, structural rewrite, and SQL Profile recommendation generation<

conclusion.a: This project demonstrates more than SQL tuning itself: it demonstrates the design and implementation of an automated SQL tuning system that models advisor lifecycle, analysis workflow, metadata persistence, recommendation generation, and optimizer-facing profile application.
conclusion.b: It also highlights hands-on experience in C++, PL/SQL, database internals, optimizer behavior, and performance engineering.

erp-database.main: A project to move seven years of data managed in Excel and CSV files into a database — database design, data migration, and a DB monitoring dashboard.

summary.b: Schema designed in recurring sessions with the operations and merchandising owners.
summary.c: Migration code that bulk-inserts every accumulated file into the database.
summary.d: 16 scheduled batches keep the DB current as new files keep arriving.

domain.desc: Five domains, each with its own naming convention and lifecycle. The DB console classifies every table by these prefixes.

migration.code: Master tables loaded first, then their dependent tables grouped and run one stage at a time — each stage isolated so one failure never blocks the rest.
migration.backfill: Years of Excel/CSV loaded with idempotent UPSERT — a re-run repairs data instead of duplicating it. The same path became the daily incremental load.
migration.partition: Data loaded daily by date (sales, purchases, logs) is list-partitioned by store so no single table grows unbounded.

batch.a: 16 batches spread across the night (02:00–06:30) and an evening polling window, time-separated so heavy loads never overlap.
batch.b: Fallback logic for each failure case (missing file, changed format, and so on), plus backfill logic that always re-checks the previous day and fills in what is missing.
batch.c: A batch monitoring dashboard that surfaces the state of every job, with issue alerts and manual re-runs where operators need them.

console.usage: Reads PostgreSQL catalogs directly — row estimates, table and index size, vacuum/analyze times, database growth.
console.relation: Merges live foreign keys with documented logical relations, so the model people reason about matches what the DB enforces.
console.trace: Maps all 32 ERP tabs to the tables they read — the blast radius of a schema change is visible before it ships.
console.freshness: Status and statistics for the file storage (NAS) as well as the database.

impact.ssot: Seven years of Excel/CSV replaced by one PostgreSQL database — 97 tables across 5 domains as the system of record
impact.integrity: Consistency moved from spreadsheet discipline into keys and constraints, with per-store list partitioning keeping the largest tables in check
impact.automation: 16 batches keep the DB current — fallback and backfill recover the previous day even when a file is missing or its format changes
impact.ops: A batch dashboard for alerts and manual re-runs, plus a console covering usage, relations, tab dependencies, and NAS status

agent-platform.main: To move to an AI-native development model, I designed the AI infrastructure with Harness Engineering and built a Graph Engineering system that turns each capability into a node, so they can be managed and improved in parallel.

summary.a: Harness Engineering — 46 permission rules and 7 hooks decide what the environment allows before any tool runs.
summary.b: Loop Engineering — work repeats until every story passes a fresh reviewer, not until it looks done.
summary.c: Graph Engineering — 1 subtab = 1 node = 1 agent, across 53 nodes, each with its own domain, architecture, and feedback memory.
summary.d: Each node has a single owner, so features are modified and added in parallel without collision.

pillars.harness: Governs the environment — permission tiers, guard hooks, and budgeted context injection.
pillars.graph: Decomposes the product into nodes — one subtab, one agent, shared assets as explicit edges.
pillars.loop: Repeats until verified — story-by-story iteration with reviewer sign-off before completion.

layout.desc: Everything the agents run on is version-controlled in the repo — no per-developer setup, no hidden state.

harness.desc: The environment is designed as six harnesses, each built and audited separately.
harness.context: CLAUDE.md policy plus 3-layer memory (meta / domain / service) with budgeted auto-injection.
harness.permission: deny / ask tiers in settings.json, plus hooks that block below the permission layer.
harness.tool: Skills route, agents own, commands expose — trigger-keyword collisions documented as boundaries.
harness.subagent: 4 git worktrees for filesystem isolation; the memory-sharing gap between them is documented, not hidden.
harness.verification: Regression checklists live in the skills. Creating test files is free; committing them is blocked.
harness.debugging: An environment scope matrix built without ever reading a secret value.

permission.deny: Hard denials — git push, DROP / TRUNCATE, rm -rf /, and any read or edit of .env and secrets. Approval cannot override them.
permission.ask: Confirmation required — git commit / merge / rebase, docker compose lifecycle, migrations, chmod, sudo.
permission.gate: /nas on and /danger on write a gate file holding an expiry epoch — access is granted for a window, not forever.
permission.secrets: .env is deny-read at the permission layer. The environment matrix records where each variable is declared, never its value.

hooks.desc: Seven hooks across four lifecycle events. Guards exit 2 to block; memory hooks fail open so they can never stall a session.
hooks.recall: Scores memory files against the prompt by IDF and injects the best match under a 4,000-character budget.
hooks.nas: Blocks any command carrying a production NAS marker unless the gate is open.
hooks.danger: Blocks irreversible commands — force push, reset --hard, docker prune, SQL drop / truncate.
hooks.testfile: Creating test files is free; committing them is blocked. Added after 859 lines of unrequested tests shipped inside a feature commit.
hooks.initsql: Detects DDL/DML run in a session and requires init.sql — the schema source of truth — to mirror it.
hooks.sync: Keeps plugin definitions in sync after edits to them.
hooks.consolidate: If the session took a correction but nothing was recorded, it prompts once before exit.

graph.desc: Development happens per node, not per repository. A node is one subtab with one owning agent, so a change stays inside its boundary.
graph.node: 53 agents map 1:1 onto subtabs, each carrying its own domain, architecture, and feedback memory.
graph.parallel: Independent nodes are delegated in a single message and run at once — several features change without collision.
graph.edge: Shared formulas, API response keys, and DB tables are the edges. Touching one requires reporting back to the main session.
graph.build: A new node and its edges are generated by agent-blueprint from a reference node — never invented from scratch.

impact.safety: Destructive and production-reaching commands are blocked below the approval layer, with access granted only through expiring gates
impact.repeatability: A new tab's agent system is scaffolded from one reference structure instead of being invented each time
impact.knowledge: Corrections become numbered feedback entries that are re-injected into later sessions automatically
impact.discipline: Every enforcement claim in the docs was verified against the code, and the gaps were fixed rather than described

erp-architecture.main: An in-house ERP that automates purchasing, inventory, ordering and settlement for 10 apparel retail stores. This page is not a feature tour — it is the record of how the architecture was decided: start from quality attributes and constraints, compare alternatives, and write down what each choice bought and what it cost, across 8 ADRs.

summary.a: Vendors and POS drop files; the system cleans and judges them overnight and produces per-store order sheets (.xls) and 60 operating tabs by morning. Neither the input nor the output is a human — both are files.
summary.b: Scalability was deliberately left off the quality list. The complexity that horizontal scaling would have cost was spent on accuracy and change velocity instead — the single largest directional choice here.
summary.c: 8 decisions are recorded as ADRs, and every record states the cost alongside the benefit. A record with an empty consequences section has not recorded a decision.
summary.d: The 9 debt items are side effects of decisions, not mistakes. Each one carries the signal that re-opens its ADR.

flow.desc: Technology was never picked straight off the business goal. Goals were lowered into architecture drivers (core function, quality attributes, constraints); alternatives that could satisfy those drivers were compared at three levels — tactic, style, pattern; the trade-off that the comparison exposed was stated; and only then was the decision made. Only the significant ones become ADRs.

lens.desc: These three words get used interchangeably. Taking this project's caching decision as the example: a tactic says what to do, a pattern says in what shape, and the trade-off says what you hand over in return.
lens.tactic: Judgement and aggregation are far too heavy to compute inside a single request. Read performance is bought by precomputing rather than by optimising code. At this point it is a direction, not yet a structure.
lens.pattern: That tactic is realised as roughly 30 precomputed tables filled by the nightly batch. Loading is DELETE→INSERT keyed on snapshot_date — a same-day rerun overwrites, and days accumulate. The web layer only reads.
lens.tradeoff: Freshness now depends on the batch succeeding. When a batch fails the screen does not error — it quietly shows yesterday's value. That is exactly why batch observability and an explicit "data as-of" stamp stop being optional.

func.ingest: Vendors and POS expose no query API — only CSV, XLS and XLSX files. 13 ingest batches are the only way data enters, which is why the batch layer is the root of the system.
func.judge: Returns, transfers, samples, payout rate and order scoring are all judged overnight. These are analytical computations — regression, percentile, FIFO lot allocation — and cannot sit on the request path.
func.order: Order sheets for 8 store types are written as legacy .xls (BIFF). The downstream purchasing system requires that format, so there is no choice to make.
func.console: 60 operating tabs across 13 groups, plus permissions. It is the window for judgement and monitoring, not the origin of the data.

qa.desc: A quality attribute is not what the system does but how well it must do it. The ranking exists for one reason — to decide in advance which quality yields when two of them collide. Every later decision is judged against this order.

accuracy.s: The same metric read from two different tabs must return the same number. Purchase amounts and settlement ride on it; once values diverge, trust in the whole system is gone.
accuracy.r: Single source of truth · one shared module per formula · no duplicated judgement logic

freshness.s: Opening a dashboard at the start of the working day shows values through the previous day's close, with the data as-of date displayed alongside.
freshness.r: Nightly precompute · batch run-history table · as-of date on screen

velocity.s: When the business asks for a change to a judgement rule, it ships the same day after approval. Frontend changes apply with no restart at all.
velocity.r: Buildless · bind-mount deploy · per-tab isolation · three-layer split

readperf.s: Opening a heavy judgement tab renders immediately by reading precomputed rows — no recomputation.

ops.s: If the app process dies, the container restarts itself and self-checks the schema. Time spent on infrastructure stays minimal.
ops.r: 2 nodes · 3 container types · restart: unless-stopped · unattended deploy

qa.noscale: There are a few dozen internal users, 10 stores, and a few hundred thousand rows a day. The complexity a scale-out design would have demanded — statelessness, distributed cache, externalised sessions, service decomposition — was spent on accuracy and change velocity instead. Scalability is absent from the list by decision, not by oversight.

const.desc: These could not be changed. Most of the decisions that follow are consequences of these constraints, not preferences.

source.c: Vendors and POS deliver data only as files (CSV · XLS · XLSX). No query API.
source.e: Ingest batches are the only entry point → the batch layer becomes the root of the system

output.c: The downstream purchasing system requires legacy .xls (BIFF)
output.e: No choice of format → xlwt is mandatory and the server must generate files

hw.c: Two self-hosted nodes (koclo-vm · NAS). No cloud budget.
hw.e: Vertical scaling only → designed around a single process and one DB per node

net.c: No inbound ports may be opened
net.e: Cloudflare tunnel dials out · the CI runner is self-hosted and dials out too

biz.c: Judgement rules (returns · transfers · samples · payout rate) change every season
biz.e: Formulas touch code often → deployment friction must stay near zero

verify.c: Review and test procedures already exist — changes are filtered before deployment
verify.e: Little left for a build step to catch → no heavy build is introduced

alt.desc: Once the drivers are fixed, alternatives surface at three levels. A tactic is the means that buys a quality; a style is the skeleton that is hard to undo once chosen; a pattern is a proven solution at a narrower scope. Mixing the levels is what makes "why was it built this way" unanswerable.

tactic.desc: The means chosen per quality attribute. Still a direction, not yet a structure.
tactic.time: Read performance — move heavy computation off the request and onto the night. Solved by splitting the time axis, not by optimising code.
tactic.ssot: Accuracy — reduce the integration point to a single database. With no queue, no RPC and no shared file between batch and web, there is nowhere for values to diverge.
tactic.idem: Data integrity — processing the same file twice must not change the result. Recovery stays simple only when rerunning is safe.
tactic.obs: Observability — the four signals are not collected continuously; collection is switched on for a named target when needed, and the session expires on its own.

style.desc: The skeleton. What was rejected explains more than what was adopted.
style.layered: One tab is three files — service (pure computation), router (JSON I/O), Vue (presentation). The server never renders HTML, and the presentation layer never computes.
style.cs: The SPA consumes JSON only. With no server templates, a screen change is decoupled from a server restart.
style.pipeline: The batch layer and the web layer differ in process, driver and time of day, and meet only at a table. A failure on one side does not stop the other.
style.rejected: At a few dozen users and 10 stores, service decomposition and an event bus make accuracy harder to hold, not easier. Boundary consistency, eventual consistency and distributed tracing cost more than they return here.

pattern.desc: Proven solutions to specific design problems. Applied narrowly, only where needed.
pattern.read: Judgement results land in ~30 precomputed tables and the web only reads them. The write model and the read model are separated — but it stops short of event sourcing.
pattern.upsert: Idempotency takes three forms depending on the data — ON CONFLICT upsert for accumulating time series, ranged DELETE+INSERT for sliding windows, TRUNCATE and reload for tables where only the current state matters.
pattern.cache: The server forces revalidation on static files, and CSS and entry scripts break versions with a manual ?v= stamp. The service worker deliberately caches nothing, because caching would defeat both of the other two defences at once.
pattern.tunnel: The host dials outward and receives domain traffic over that connection. Zero inbound ports, no certificate renewal. The CI runner dials out on the same principle.

runtime.desc: Put the decisions together and this is the shape that results. The write flow at night and the read flow by day differ in process, driver and time of day, and share nothing but tables. One integration point is why values cannot diverge — and also why a failure on one side can stay silent.

tradeoff.desc: The trade-off is what surfaces once the alternatives are compared. If the right-hand column of a row is empty, that row recorded a preference, not a decision.

pre.gain: A tab query becomes a single indexed SELECT. Response characteristics hold as the number of screens grows, and per-date time-series tracking comes along for free.
pre.cost: Freshness now depends on batch success. Changing a judgement rule does not change the screen until the rebuild runs. And because these tables must stay re-creatable, foreign keys are kept shallow (45 FKs across 150 tables).

build.gain: Frontend edits apply instantly with no rebuild and no restart. The code in the browser is the code in the repository, so debugging works without source maps.
build.cost: No tree shaking and no bundle splitting, so desktop views are not lazily loaded. Type checking and linting cannot be enforced on the deployment path — the pre-merge procedure carries that instead.

mount.gain: Deployment takes seconds and CI has no build or push step. Fewer failure points, and a clear boundary: only what can be undone is automated.
mount.cost: The image is no longer the truth of a deployment. Rollback by reverting to one reproducible artifact does not apply — reverting means a git revert plus a restart.

migrate.gain: No tool to learn, no version conflicts, no rollback scripts to maintain. A re-creatable derived table is simply dropped and rebuilt.
migrate.cost: The schema source of truth (init.sql) is a mirror that never executes, so it can fall behind reality. With three application paths, how far a change has propagated is not visible at a glance.

proc.gain: The cache warmer, task worker and scheduler each run exactly once — no duplicate-suppression machinery needed. The failure mode where a dead reloader keeps serving stale code is structurally impossible.
proc.cost: Vertical scaling only, and a brief downtime on each restart. One heavy synchronous call can block every response, so it relies on the discipline of offloading to a thread.

tunnel.gain: Zero inbound ports. Firewall rules, port forwarding and certificate renewal disappear entirely, and TLS termination is handled outside.
tunnel.cost: An external service becomes a single point of failure. With no proxy layer, static caching, rate limiting and IP allowlisting all land in application middleware.

tradeoff.summary: This architecture bought speed by converting "what a tool enforced" into "what people must uphold" — the optimisation a bundler did, the ordering guarantee a migration tool did, the regression detection CI did. That is why development conventions and the harness are not an accessory here; they are part of the architecture.

adr.desc: One decision, one record. Each record has four sections — context, alternatives, decision, consequences — and the consequences state the cost accepted, not only the benefit gained.

a1.context: Input is vendor-dropped CSV, XLS and XLSX; the final artifact is a legacy .xls order sheet. Everything between them is analytical work — aggregation, weighted regression, percentiles, FIFO lot allocation — not CRUD. The place where code piles up is the data layer, not the web layer.
a1.alt: Pick the web framework first (Node or JVM) and fit data processing around it. That path means building the legacy .xls read/write and analytics ecosystem yourself, or splitting it into a separate process.
a1.decision: Build the whole backend on Python + FastAPI. Data processing uses pandas, openpyxl, xlrd and xlwt, with the web layer laid thinly on top. The data tooling was chosen first and the web was placed on it — not the other way round.
a1.gain: The mature legacy .xls read/write ecosystem is used as-is. API and batch share one language and one module, so a formula like backorder merging lives in a single file and cannot diverge.
a1.cost: The runtime is at a disadvantage for CPU-bound work. Synchronous libraries (pandas, psycopg2) block the event loop inside an async app unless they are handed to a separate thread.

a2.context: This is a UI newly introduced to the shop floor, so real usage feedback keeps arriving and judgement rules change each season — screens are edited constantly. Meanwhile change quality is already assured by review and test procedures, leaving little for a build step to catch.
a2.alt: Adopt a bundler (Vite, webpack). It buys optimisation and type checking, but the deployed artifact then differs from the source, forcing a redesign of the whole chain — cache invalidation, restart decisions, emergency fixes.
a2.decision: No bundler, no node_modules, no build step. Libraries load as CDN scripts and application code as native ES modules. The rule is written into the development standard as a non-negotiable item.
a2.gain: Frontend edits apply immediately with no restart and no rebuild — deployment friction is effectively zero. The version, vulnerability and supply-chain burden of a Node toolchain disappears entirely.
a2.cost: No tree shaking, bundle splitting or minification. Type checking and linting cannot be enforced on the deployment path, and module cache invalidation rests on a single layer of server revalidation.

a3.context: ADR-002 fixed the buildless constraint first. But the screens are not simple documents — 60 tabs, nested sub-tabs, and large tables and charts carrying sort, filter, modal and selection state. The earlier approach of embedding generated HTML in iframes had already hit its limit.
a3.alt: React (assumes JSX) · Angular (assumes AOT compilation) · server templates with partial updates. The first two are incompatible with the buildless constraint; the last cannot carry this much client state.
a3.decision: Load Vue 3 as the CDN global build and write components as string templates in .js files. One argument settled it — the global build ships the runtime template compiler, giving a complete component model with no build step.
a3.gain: A full SPA-grade UI without giving up ADR-002. iframe tabs could be migrated one at a time, so the transition was incremental rather than a rewrite.
a3.cost: Shipping the runtime compiler makes the runtime larger and moves template compilation into the browser. String templates give up editor support and compile-time error detection — typos surface at runtime.

a4.context: When the same number lives in both a file cache and the database, there is no way to say which is right — and the moment only one side updates, screens start disagreeing quietly. At the same time, returns, transfers, scoring and payout-rate judgement are far too heavy for one request. Consistency and responsiveness had to hold at once.
a4.alt: Keep the file cache alongside the source of truth (leaves room for values to diverge) · compute on request (gives up response time) · introduce a separate OLAP engine (complexity out of proportion to the operations headcount).
a4.decision: Route all data through one PostgreSQL instance and remove the file cache from the set of truths. Heavy judgement is computed by the nightly batch into ~30 precomputed tables that the web layer only reads. Loading is DELETE→INSERT per snapshot_date, satisfying same-day idempotency and per-date accumulation at once.
a4.gain: There is nowhere left for values to diverge — batch and web read the same rows. A tab query is one indexed SELECT, and because days accumulate, time-series tracking and after-the-fact verification come for free.
a4.cost: Freshness depends on batch success, so a failure shows a stale value rather than an error. Changing judgement logic does nothing until a rebuild runs, and foreign keys stay shallow to keep the tables re-creatable.

a5.context: A large share of the 150 tables are derived, re-creatable precomputed tables. A conventional migration tool assumes a version chain, but for tables that can be dropped and rebuilt at any time that chain buys little. The operations headcount is also small.
a5.alt: Adopt a migration tool such as Alembic. It buys ordering guarantees and rollback scripts, but binds even derived tables into the version chain and adds learning and operating cost.
a5.decision: No migration tool. The schema source of truth is init.sql at the repository root, and it reaches databases along three paths — init.sql once for a new database; hand-written SQL files or ensure_schema() at app startup for existing ones; and self-creation inside some ingest batches.
a5.gain: No tool to learn, no version conflicts, no rollback scripts to maintain. Thanks to ensure_schema(), a good share of changes apply themselves on the next startup after deployment.
a5.cost: The source of truth is a mirror that never executes, so it can fall behind reality, and with three application paths the current state is not visible at a glance. The ordering convention — apply the migration before the code — rests on people; a hook that detects DDL execution mitigates it.

a6.context: Deployment is frequent (2,054 commits), there is no container registry, and there are two target hosts whose build capacity is not generous. Meanwhile almost every change is Python source or frontend files, and dependencies barely move.
a6.alt: Rebuild the image and push to a registry on every deploy. It buys a reproducible artifact and a clean rollback, but drags registry operations and build time straight into the deployment cycle.
a6.decision: Use the image as a dependency shell only and bind-mount application code read-only from a host path. Whether to restart is decided automatically from the changed path — only backend/app/** triggers a restart, while dependency, image, compose and schema changes only warn and are handed to a person.
a6.gain: Deployment takes seconds and frontend changes need no restart at all. With no build or push step, the pipeline is simple, and the boundary is explicit: only what can be undone is automated.
a6.cost: The image is not the truth of a deployment, so artifact-level rollback does not apply. A library present in the image but not pinned in the dependency list stays invisible, and a dirty host working tree halts the deploy.

a7.context: With a few dozen internal users there is little need for multiple workers, while the app runs a cache warmer, a task worker and a scheduler inside the process — adding workers would run each of them more than once. The container also has large NAS shares mounted.
a7.alt: Multiple workers (gunicorn) with auto-reload. It buys throughput and developer convenience, but requires duplicate-suppression for background tasks, and a file watcher that dies while watching large mounts leaves stale code being served.
a7.decision: Run uvicorn as a single foreground process with auto-reload disabled. Code changes take effect only through an explicit restart. On 2026-09-11 the second HTTPS process was removed, consolidating to one process.
a7.gain: Background tasks run exactly once. The failure mode where a dead reloader keeps serving old code becomes structurally impossible.
a7.cost: Vertical scaling only, so throughput is capped by a single core, and each restart carries a brief downtime. One heavy synchronous call can block every response.

a8.context: No inbound port can be opened on the production host, and there is neither a static IP nor anyone to operate certificates. Yet store staff need mobile access from outside the office.
a8.alt: An nginx or caddy reverse proxy with opened ports, port forwarding and automated certificate renewal. It buys layered routing and static caching, but collides head-on with the no-inbound constraint.
a8.decision: No reverse proxy. A Cloudflare tunnel establishes the connection outward from the host and forwards domain traffic to localhost:9000. The CI runner dials out to GitHub from inside the host on the same principle.
a8.gain: Zero inbound ports. Firewall rules, port forwarding and certificate renewal disappear entirely, and TLS termination and DDoS mitigation are handled externally.
a8.cost: An external service becomes a single point of failure. With no proxy layer the app absorbs static caching, rate limiting and layered routing itself — which is why static serving and IP allowlisting live in application middleware.

debt.desc: The debt accumulated by the decisions above. Each item is a side effect of a decision rather than a mistake, and when its re-open signal fires, the corresponding ADR is reconsidered.

schema.w: Writing production DDL back into the source of truth is a human task, so the source of truth can fall behind reality. With three application paths, propagation state is hard to see at a glance.
schema.s: When a fresh environment will not start from the source of truth alone — re-evaluate adopting a migration tool

fresh.w: When a batch fails, the screen shows a stale value rather than an error. That failures can be silent is an intrinsic property of this structure.
fresh.s: When a case surfaces where the as-of stamp or failure notification did not reach anyone

load.w: Desktop views are not lazily loaded, so a first visit downloads code for tabs that will never be opened. The only code splitting today is the mobile views.
load.s: When initial load is reported as a problem over a store's connection

verify.w: Verification happens before merge — four-dimension code review, a post-verification skill, and verification scripts. The deployment pipeline does not check any of it again.
verify.s: When a change that bypassed the procedure causes an incident — re-evaluate adding a gate to the pipeline

layer.w: Most routers are thin, but a few older ones still hold SQL directly, blurring the boundary between computation and I/O.
layer.s: Push it down into the service layer the next time that router is opened

node.w: Both nodes receive the same commit but each keeps its own database. Both respond, so the fact that something responded does not tell you which node you were looking at.
node.s: When a value check goes wrong through node confusion — pin the target at the pipeline level

debt.summary: The whole list reduces to one sentence — speed was bought by converting what a tool enforced into what people must uphold. That is why development conventions and the harness are not an accessory here; they are part of the architecture.

impact.consistency: Reducing the integration point to a single database structurally removes the class of bug where one metric disagrees between tabs
impact.velocity: Buildless plus bind-mount deployment means frontend changes need no restart and backend changes ship in seconds
impact.ops: Two nodes and three container types keep the operating surface small, with deploy, restart decisions and health checks unattended
impact.trace: 8 decisions and 9 debt items recorded with their ADRs and re-open signals, so "why this structure" survives as evidence rather than as prose
